sign_convention.positive_angle: swings a downward-hanging part's tip toward +x (forward)

canonical_rig.T0436_source: @DennieSeth's skeleton reference, zorder_fix_2026-10-08/dennie_canonical_skeleton_ref.png. That file is not present in this worktree or this card's attachments -- every number below is transcribed from the task card's own body/comment (which record it as measured by seeding the image and snapping to the drawn strokes, confirmed by 1px scanline for the two bars), not re-derived from the source pixels by this round. See docs/design/23-canonical-rig.md "Where these numbers came from."

leg_proportions.projection_reasoning: In this lunge the near thigh points away from the viewer (compressed) while the near shin crosses the view plane (full length), so the near-side ratio (1.78) is a projection artifact rather than anatomy; the far-side ratio (1.11) sits inside the anatomical range (1.0-1.1) and is adopted instead. This REVERSES the general near-side-is-truth rule for THIS pose's legs only -- that rule still holds for the arms (upper_limb_reference_comparison below).
leg_proportions.why_not_applied: thigh_R/calf_R (mirrored to thigh_L/calf_L) already drive the leg geometry of every existing animation (walk_cycle, idle_cycle, sitting_idle_cycle); rescaling them to the adopted fractions would shorten every one of those legs by roughly a third, which is exactly the animation re-derivation this card's scope excludes. Recorded here as the target for the follow-on cards that re-derive each animation's own leg geometry.

upper_limb_reference_comparison.note: Upper arm is already close to the reference (within 0.03 of spine, 'already right'); forearm is about +30% over. Neither is corrected this round, for the same reason as leg_proportions.why_not_applied -- every existing animation drives its forearm length from this same rig entry, and rescaling it is the follow-on cards' business.

lateral_offset_axis.description: A per-part, opt-in sideways (local-x) displacement -- rig_compositor.build_placements's lateral_offset_frac parameter, expressed as a fraction of the torso's own width. Distinct from z-order: z decides which part wins a contested pixel, this moves the pixel itself. Every part defaults to 0.0 (no displacement, no behaviour change) unless named in a caller's own dict; no existing pose module (walk_cycle, idle_cycle, sitting_idle_cycle) passes this parameter, so none of them is affected by this axis existing.
lateral_offset_axis.demonstration_values_note: FIX ROUND 2 (docs/design/23-canonical-rig.md Sec 3c): fix round 1 (@DennieSeth, 2026-10-08T21:08) equalized the two arm-chain parts and the two leg-chain parts to the same value per chain, correctly diagnosing that four DIFFERENT per-part offsets tear a chain apart -- but rig_compositor.build_placements still applied the offset twice per chain (once inherited through forward kinematics from the root, once again explicitly at the distal part's own name), so the equalized dict values still produced a DOUBLED effective shift at the distal part (measured: the arm chain's distal part moved -0.700 x torso vs its root's -0.350 x torso, exactly 2x). The reviewer's FAIL verdict (2026-10-08T21:54:30Z) caught this by direct measurement. This round removes the second, redundant lateral() application in rig_compositor.build_placements -- the offset is now applied exactly once, at each chain's root, and the distal part inherits it purely through FK, so equal dict values now produce an equal effective shift. A consequence: the chain is now rigid and cannot tear at any magnitude, so the real risk is the whole chain detaching from the main body, not a tear partway along it -- re-swept directly against the fixed code (4-connectivity component labelling): the arm chain first detaches a new >=50px fragment at a magnitude of 1.00 (none through 0.95), the leg chain at 0.80 (none through 0.70). These bounds were swept on the ARM/LEG CHAIN as a whole, independent of which named side (`_L` or `_R`) carries the value -- see fix_round_6_note and fix_round_7_note for why the side/name changed.
lateral_offset_axis.fix_round_5_note: @DennieSeth's fix-round-5 comment measured the fix-round-2 arm-chain value (-0.35, then on shoulder_L/forearm_L -- fix round 5 predates the fix-round-6 near/far swap and the fix-round-7 name swap below) against the SHOULDER JOINT ITSELF, not just the silhouette: it opens a wedge of background in the armhole (between the far shoulder and torso, within 130px of the shoulder joint) because the sleeve is pushed clear of the torso entirely -- the earlier sweep (fix round 2, above) only checked for NEW detached blobs, never the armhole gap. A uniform part up-scale does not close it: the part is pinned at its own pivot (the proximal/shoulder end), so scaling only extends the DISTAL end further out -- the sleeve-to-torso gap is unaffected by scale, only by this offset. Re-swept directly against the fixed code (with the width-restore anisotropic scale already applied, so these are the actual committed sleeve geometry, not the pre-fix isotropic one), magnitude (unsigned) vs armhole wedge px / sleeve-torso overlap px / (shoulder + forearm) visible px on the far side AS NAMED AT THAT TIME: 0.35: 3322 / 166 / 23963, 0.25: 1482 / 1274 / 22824, 0.16: 516 / 2982 / 21096, 0.10: 184 / 4523 / 19580, 0.05: 52 / 5865 / 18231. Chosen magnitude: 0.10, bracketed on both sides -- 0.05 leaves only 231px of margin above the 18000px far-arm-visibility floor (too close to the edge of the far arm being hidden again), while 0.16 and above reopen the armhole past the 400px ceiling. 0.10 keeps a comfortable margin on both bounds (184px of 400 on the wedge side, 1580px of margin above the 18000px floor on the visibility side) while the far shoulder genuinely overlaps the torso (4523px) rather than merely abutting it. NOTE (fix round 7): these specific pixel counts were measured against the PRE-fix-round-6 part identity and are retained verbatim as a historical record of how the magnitude 0.10 was chosen; they are superseded as a CURRENT measurement by fix_round_6_note's and fix_round_7_note's own re-measurements below, which found a different armhole-wedge number (340px, not 184px) against the actual committed geometry -- see fix_round_7_note for the correction.
lateral_offset_axis.fix_round_6_note: @DennieSeth chose Option B (2026-10-09T16:43): the two limb-chain groups swap z-order wholesale (see rig.*.z above), so `_L` was the NEAR side (drawn in front) and `_R` was the FAR side for the remainder of fix round 6 -- the reverse of every prior round, where the lateral offset lived on `_L`. The offset's PURPOSE is unchanged -- clear the FAR limb from the torso's own silhouette -- so it moved to the parts that were then far: `shoulder_R`/`forearm_R` (magnitude unchanged at 0.10, sign flipped to +0.10 since the far side then sat screen-right of the hip) and `thigh_R`/`calf_R` (magnitude unchanged at 0.06, sign flipped to +0.06). CORRECTION (fix round 7, superseding the claim this note made at the time): re-measured directly against the fix-round-6 committed rig, the armhole wedge was 340px and the far-arm (shoulder_R + forearm_R) visible count was 18692px -- NOT the 184px/19580px this note originally claimed by assuming the fix-round-5 numbers transferred unchanged. They don't transfer unchanged: shoulder_R (fix round 6's far side) carries NO bone_length_fix entry, while shoulder_L (fix round 5's far side) carried the anisotropic height/width correction -- two different PNGs with different raw geometry, so the same offset magnitude produces different armhole/visibility numbers on each. Per-side arm angles (Sec 3e) did NOT swap with this z-order move -- Option B kept `R` reaching forward and `L` trailing back, exactly as fix round 4 measured from the reference.
